review:
The best medieval-ish city builder. I happen to be a historian specialising in the Middle Ages, and games that market themselves as “historically authentic” often leave a lot to be desired as such games often don’t even try to emulate the time period beyond basic aesthetics. Since a lot of the hype around Manor Lords comes from its commitment to historical accuracy, I'll be reviewing it from that perspective. This game, although there is room for improvement, is clearly an earnest attempt to enable players to recreate reasonably authentic medieval towns and villages and gets closer to that goal than any of its rivals. After spending about a dozen hours building a large town, it's very much unfinished but what's there is good. 

There is currently one map with some RNG elements, such as your starting location and the starting location of a rival lord who also wants this land and whom you will eventually have to fight. You will build houses which can, as was typical in the Middle Ages, have a productive plot of land to the rear for a vegetable garden or household animals like goats or a chicken coop, and the system for building them is intuitive, flexible, and a joy to use. You’ll have to manage trade with off-map settlements as well as maintain a militia to deal with bandits or the rival lord. On the whole, I really like it. 

There are some issues with the mechanics of the game:


[strike] 1. There is no way (that I can find) to limit the production of certain goods without micromanaging employment. It would be good to say “have a stockpile of 50” like you can in other settlement management games, and like you can with the trading system. I would like to not have to micromanage 14 houses just to regulate what planks are used for. [/strike] This has now been fixed, great job. 

2. Combat is trivial assuming rough parity between the size of the armies. You have to try to lose a battle to lose a battle. 

3. Bandit raids on your village happen off screen a lot of the time. Like, you can’t defend your settlement, you just get a notification that you’ve lost goods to bandits. Let us defend ourselves please, or let us have a bailiff to reign in the thieves. 

[strike] 4. Trade is overpowered, you can get to a point where the player can run the whole settlement through trade. Trade has no risks, so the game steers the player toward relying on trade rather than managing their villages. [/strike] This has been overcorrected and dealt with in the wrong way I think. Trade is now a great way to completely wreck your regional economy because you'll be exporting tools and warbows for 5 gold while bringing in barley at 12 gold a bushel. 

5. The rival lord expands far too aggressively, even on its lowest settings. By the time you can claim a single neighboring parcel of land, you’ll be lucky not to have been boxed in completely. The AI takes one parcel a year, there are 8 provinces, and it starts with two while you start with one. This means that by year 5 the AI has the map locked down entirely while you’re still trying to get a decent harvest in. This sucks and is the game’s biggest problem right now. It has been toned down a bit but I still feel unable to compete. 


The game has a remarkable ability to enable the player to create authentic medieval town layouts, and you could probably recreate some medieval towns in the game pretty accurately. However, the game seems to be based on central Europe around 1400, so it does tend to lean toward villages and towns from that time and place. While you can emulate, for example, Norman town planning with its focus on commercial high/fore streets, you cannot build a medieval Italian town in this game because plazas are not a thing (yet), while building a village around a central green would be aesthetic rather than the functional heart of the village. 

This leads on to an area where the game and its commitment to historical accuracy will hopefully improve as development continues, which is forest and land management. In most medieval-ish town planning games (this one included) you put down a logging hut and they just cut down trees, then a forester plants new trees. This is not how medieval people generally managed their woodland, if only because it’s remarkably inefficient prior to mechanised forestry. Although the villages are historically authentic, the same effort has not been put into those villages’ relationship with the land (yet). Some suggestions:

1. Coppicing. Coppicing was the practise of cutting a tree down to the stump to stimulate the growth of shoots around the stump, essentially tricking one tree into growing many trees. This would result in a large amount of harvestable wood within 7-10 years. However, the shoots were vulnerable to being eaten by deer. It has been used as a means to harvest firewood in Europe for over 1000 years. 

2. Pollarding. The same idea as coppicing, but it’s done about 2m up the tree trunk. You get less wood that’s harder to access, but deer won’t eat it. 

3. Deeper deer management. Of course, if deer keep eating everything you could just kill all the deer. Deer culling was (and still is) an important part of forestry. Although the game does have deer management it is as simple as “don’t over-hunt”. It would be good to see this expanded to reflect the real world impacts of deer overpopulation or underpopulation.

4. Wolf management. When creating new villages, they often encroached on the habitats of wolves. Wolves don't usually attack people, but if they get used to human contact and become habituated, they do. A mechanic for wolf packs similar to deer migration (except rather than going further away when bothered, they attack) might work well. It would be nice to fight something other than the tropey RNG bandit camp. 

It’s got a lot of promise, I’m sure I’ll enjoy sinking hundreds of hours into it over the years, but you might want to wait a year or so until it’s further along development.

[b][u]Before you play:[/u][/b]


— Set FPS to a multiple of 30 (30, 60, 120, etc).
— Turn off Anti-aliasing on older cards.
— Set V sync to on.
— The game sets graphics to ultra by default, lower them to medium or high to prevent sudden stuttering.


[b][u]=====Getting Your Feet Wet=====[/u][/b]


— Comments are enabled on this review, if you have a question that isn't answered here,
     leave a comment and I'll check back and try to answer it for you, then update the guide for future players.




— Play the first free build campaign first.
    much of this guide won't make a lot of sense until you get your foot into a campaign and just 'start playing'
    follow the in-game tool-tips as best as you can and when you inevitably get stuck, come back to the guide and find the section you need.


— Some resources are seasonal so assign your labor / unassign your labour accordingly, don't have families doing nothing.
— Make sure you move your starting resources into a granary/storehouse before they're damaged by weather.
— Construct your farms + Plots in November - Jan -  so they're ready to plant by spring (march)
— Don't be afraid to force-harvest fields (especially larger ones) so the crops aren't ruined by rain.
— when setting up a trading post - you can trade Firewood + Stone without opening a trade route.
— Taxing your citizens doesn't increase your regional wealth (spending cash) it increases your treasury, setting a tax early in the game isn't usually beneficial focus on establishing trade.


— How to make clothes cheaply:
 Burgher plot with goats /hunting camp - > Produces hides - > Tanner - >Level 2 Burgher plot Cobbler/tailor (shoes count as clothes)


— How to make Ale for taverns: 
 Barley field - > Malt house - > Lv2 Burgher plot with Brewery - > Tavern.


— How to farm efficiently:

—Assigning 8 people to one farming home makes little sense, you're better off assigning 2 families to a few farming houses each and giving them each an ox.
— several smaller farming fields are significantly more efficient than one large field.
— Always plant no earlier than march.
— Always Harvest by September (if you haven't got a huge amount of families at the farm, don't be afraid to 
     force an early harvest so the stock isn't ruined by weather)
— Rotate the crops yourself, don't set up a rotation or they'll plant during the wrong months.


— Building a church is an easy increase in approval.
— Building a market is an easy increase in approval.
    (you will need more than one market plot as your houses increase out of range.)
— Building multiple storehouses/granaries is necessary as you expand
— Building a well close to farming plots/houses optimises walking time.


— Assign multiple workers to granaries/Storehouses to have industry stocks/food picked up quicker.
— Try to make your burgher plots into districts and work your industry buildings around them E.G Brewers 
     near a granary, granary near a tavern, Vege farmers near a granary, Blacksmiths near a storehouse etc.
— click on your storehouses and granaries to see what the people are doing via the people tab, if they're all 
     sitting in stalls it might be time to make a new storehouse and granary to keep goods coming in.


— Place industry buildings close to a storehouse for efficiency.
— Place food sources close to a granary for efficiency.
— When trying to optimize what your storehouse and granary collect/store based on the closest goods, go to 
     the advanced tab, and deselect the goods you don't want those storage facilities to collect so they always 
     stay collecting optimal, close-distanced goods.
— Utilise roads - they're free and make Oxen and Handcarts travel quicker.
— Upgrade your hitching post and order an extra ox when you start making Wealth from trading.
— Goods that are in 'generic storage' at their production building or burgher plot are not safe from weather 
  until they are placed in a granary or storehouse.
— Each member of a family can only move 1 item at a time unless they specifically work at storehouse or 
     granary, it is ALWAYS more efficient to have enough granary/store workers to keep up with what your 
     buildings are producing than it is to have your families stop their tasks and have to transport goods 
     because their generic storage is full.


— Build extra hitching posts near logging camps/farms when you have the funds.
— Every 30 days you can order a new ox (provided you have space)
— Many buildings share the ox, so getting several of them should be a priority when you start getting some wealth.
— It is more efficient to have larger homes producing vegetables than farming.
— L-shaped or Triangle Burgher plots for farming have significantly higher yields than square-shaped blocks a lot of the time.
— You can use a Road to provide shape to L or Triangle-shaped plots.
— You can use a field to clear an area of trees if they're in the way/blocking your vision.
— Don't be afraid to delete/destroy empty market stalls so the family members running them return to doing something useful.
— it's perfectly okay to stop production and re-assign workers from other tasks if you aren't using the resources from them 'right now'


— Bandit camps are different from bandit units, you can use your troops to 'claim' bandit camps and you'll get the option of choosing either treasury wealth or regional wealth - treasury wealth increases the funds you can spend on hiring mercenaries, sending the camp goods to your region will give you immediately usable regional wealth.

Early Access Review - July 9th, 2024

First off, I am going to rate this game positively, but I am mainly going to be putting criticism in this review.  I am also only going to state what is in the game when posted, and not what it could potentially have.  It's  a beautiful and fairly well optimized game.  Great for relatively casual play.  However the game does not last as long or as challenging as I would like, making the price a bit steep for what it is currently.

For me, the game has me a bit perplexed.  On one hand, I like how the management is not overwhelming for the individual towns.  On the other hand, it means there is often a lot of times where this is very little for the player to do.  A lot of people are going to over-optimize their towns, but there is really very little reason to do so as the game naturally solves the problem quite easily.  It's basically best to try and build your towns to resemble medieval towns, level 3 houses around the market, level 2 on the outskirts, and level 1 in little hamlets around the region.

The main difficulty is that you are basically forced to make every town completely self-sufficient.  It is realistic, but for unless you are in one of the two fertile regions on the map, it is very difficult to make grain crops to have a supply of bread for a whole year, leaving you weirdly more dependent off of vegetables, eggs, berries and hunting than what should be expected.  While in theory you are supposed to optimize each village to an industry, the exporting and trade system doesn't really balance out between the regions, making the small exporting towns quite rich, while population centers to be fairly poor, due to the exporting towns not needing goods from larger towns.  Due to this, the game somewhat encourages the development of only one region, then has the player just take over all of the rest, which I don't think is intentional at all.

Combat is also far simpler than I would have liked.  While arches have been buffed from early access release, they are still underwhelming.  The current combat scale is a bit too small to make positional warfare an important strategy, making the simplest strategy to just have spear militia to pin the enemy and retinue charge and break them.  Unless you can get silver VERY fast, mercenaries are largely out of the question for the player.

The other thing is that the physical map stays the same, though each time you start the game the resources and fertility are randomized.  I would recommend restarting the game until you have a starting region that you are happy with.  However, even with this, the game doesn't really encourages me to do a second playthough after fully restoring the peace.  I might build another settlement on that playthrough just to try and make a better ale production, though in reality, most likely I will just have to crash the global demand for ale with this new town just to the price is cheaper for all my other towns to import it.

Once again, I did enjoy this game.  Most of the enjoyment is from watching your town grow, and walking around.  Don't try to meta this game too hard, just try to relax and take your time with it.  Other than the occasional bandit raid or claim being pushed on you, it is actually a fairly relaxing game to wind down to once you have the necessities built and families assigned.  Further expansion of required goods and services to the towns will likely make it more interesting in the long run, as well as more diplomacy and other AI towns on a larger map.  I am willing to see where this game will head in the future, though it will likely be several more years until a more complete vision will be realized.

Also, feel free to ask me any questions on this game in the comments below, and I'll gladly answer them!

The game was incredibly promising two years ago at release and the bones are still there. It has a foundation that no other medieval city (village) building game has, and I really hope for a future where I can change this review. However, for the past two years we've gotten very little content (basically just stone castles that are frankly, not all that interesting) and just rebalance after rebalance that haven't actually changed how the game feels. Every "major" update has me saying cool while reading patchnotes, and quitting again after an hour because the "improved balance" doesn't improve the fun in any meaningful way. The communication from dev(s) has steadily dropped off to the point that the CEO of the publisher stepped in, which was promising at first but has quickly also turned lackluster because it seems there's nothing to actually report from the devs. A year ago I excused the lack of content as a responsible dev (or team, it's really unclear how many people are actually working on this game) trying to lay a stronger foundation to make integrating future content easier. However, with all the "major" reworks doing basically nothing, or undoing previous major reworks, it seems to me that the dev doesn't actually know what he wants this game to be, and is chasing himself in a circle with no direction - or the worse option, which is just doing nothing. Until I see some kind of meaningful accountability for the slow progress (besides the occasional non-apologetic tweet about game development being hard) and a good explanation from the dev for why the rebalances actually matter and should be done, I cannot recommend spending money on this game.

I myself have spent hundreds of hours in this game, albeit in custom difficulty modes. Customization is good here; I've crafted a difficulty scenario where I am not being mercilessly attacked nor having my territory taken, but fighting the AI Lord is still a challenge. That being said...

The level of depth in the Burgage plots alone is what drew me to this game. It's Banished but with real upgrades that mean something. You can build burgage plots that are just big enough for a backyard, and plan that entire family around becoming a tailor/butcher/brewer etc. to boost your economy and resource production. The fact that at level 1 these plots can be made MASSIVE and turned into a vegetable field (Or Orchard!) while simultaneously housing up to 2 families is amazing!! It allows such a wide variety of strange and natural shapes to exist within your town, and can help keep village designs from turning into grids.

The learning curve here is similar to every colony sim IMO, you just kinda have to face smash the first few colonies until you understand how to quickly setup the things necessary for a taxable village, then mercenaries and retinue can be aquired to fight the bandits and prepare for later combat with the AI Lord. The difficulty here is that if the AI Lord is "aggressive" he will be able to claim your starting territory before you can get any troops gathered, and it's kinda game over from there. Changing that setting alone will make the game much more playable. I recommend playing with just bandits for a bit to get the feel for quickly getting troops together.

The graphics are amazing, and among the best I've seen in a colony sim. The villagers hammer and saw on structures and individual beams and walls get added on as the construction goes on, which is an incredible touch. Animation of the villagers is good from afar or up close. On the larger villages (50+ level three burgage plots) you can get some chugging, but that could also be my dated CPU.

All in all this is one of my favorite colony sims I've ever played, and I eagerly await the updates. From the begining this has been a very small team, but they've always done great work and listened to the community. I get the feeling that some of the updates they are working on are more challenging than the last, but I have faith that this game will be carried through to it's potential!

Alright, so I have a love/hate relationship with this game. Its a fun game and if you wanna spend alot of time developing a nice city and doing all that then this is great for you. But somethings to be aware of:

- The economy is ****EXTREMELY**** broken. You could be selling swords, spears, helmets, boots, cloaks, veggies, beer, dyes, charcoal, wool, linen, wooden parts and both types of shields. But if you need Barley & grain it'll sink your regional wealth. Which in turn bankrupts you. So basically if you cant build a town that is 100% self sustaining then you may as well quit and start over. 
- The enemy will spawn directly into your town. Wether it be bandits or the opposing Lord. Sometimes they'll spawn other places but majority of the time they are going to spawn from off map, directly into your region. So prepare to have your town completely wiped several times a game. 

- When the off map Lord decides to attack, don't just assume you won because you won the first battle. Give it about 60 seconds and he will spawn a completely new and fresh army to attack you with. So you could of spent ridiculous amounts of money mainlining a standing army of your own, supplementing it with mercenaries, and it'll likely not be enough. So get ready to lose. Also understand that you will never have a retinue as large as his. He will have around 30+ and max you can get is like 24. Plus have several bands of mercenaries with him. Which again, will all re spawn fresh and ready to go.

- If you have mercenaries spawned on the map be prepared for your carts/oxen to get caught in them. So keep an eye on them or it'll cause a clog. 

- Resource distribution is wild in this game. A house directly next to a fully stocked market might get the resources from it. Maybe. But one a few blocks down the road will definitely get them. 

- Keep an eye on production. If you don't set limits on what your specialists make then they're going to drain every last resource you have and its not physically possible to keep up. 

- Lately unassigned workers have been disappearing. Why? who knows. You'll have 10 unassigned families and they will all disappear. 

- The villagers are MASSIVE drunks. Your most valuable resource in the entire game is ale. Everything comes to a screeching halt without it. You cant upgrade buildings. You cant get perk points. You'll lose. But again you cant really import it because it'll bankrupt you. So good luck.

- DON'T BOTHER WITH APIARIES. They are worthless and a massive waste of time. Streamers say they're great but they're lying. You get maybe 3 honey a month from them. Which is instantly gone and you don't see a benefit from it because its burnt through so fast. So do yourself a favor and pick a different perk. It doesn't matter how many you place down or how many families you assign. You re only getting a max of 3. Period. End of story. 

- Also don't bother getting the hunter traps or double meat perks. They don't work either. You cant physically produce enough meat to sustain a villages wants. So forget it altogether and focus on veggies, berries and apples. Maybe if you're lucky you might get good farm land and can grow some wheat and barley. But don't count on it. Farmers will consistently not plow half a field or wont plant most of it. I've found it best to make small .3 size plots for farming. But the problems still persist regardless of how many farmers, oxen and time you devote to it. 

For all of its flaws it is a fun game. Sometimes you'll do alright and somehow survive long enough to complete a map. But odds are you wont. Get comfortable with the idea of spending hours, even days, working on one really awesome town. Then it's going to be levels by bandits and the rival lord will take it over and then you'll have to start all over. For a single developer its a very beautiful game and has some seriously solid bones. But obvious being in early access its gonna have issues. Apparently there's a complete rework being made so maybe soon all of these issues wont even be a thing anymore. Fingers crossed cause I do enjoy it.

Finally a medieval city builder that doesn't lock everything to a grid. Manor lords positively oozes authenticity. Watching my villagers go from rags, to.. slightly fancier rags instills me with a sense of pride I have not felt from another game in a long time. From the first tree you fell, the first harvest collected, the first soldier slain defending his home; Everything adds to the compounding emotional investment in YOUR settlement. I attribute this to the fact that this game basically has zero menus or spreadsheet management windows. If you want to manage your village, you have to manually fly around and assign people to their stations. In turn you will familiarize with every nook and cranny of your growing town, watching every event unfold and endearing you to the peasants under your thumb in the process. Some might see this as a detriment, but for roleplaying nerds like myself it is a godsend, and a design choice I hope stays for good. This is a splendid foundation which has the potential to become an all-time great. I eagerly await future updates.

I cannot recommend this game in its current form or any form to be expected in the foreseeable future. I bought the game at early access release in April 2024, I believe for $30. It looks like it has increased to $40 now - laughable when it has arguably less replayability now than it had at launch. Development speed is abhorrent for a game that has $50+ million in revenue. When you generate that much money (even if you started as a single developer) and you have accomplished so little in 2.5 years of early access, it really starts to feel like a rug pull.

After a year of complete silence the dev team released a patch and a public apology for poor communication after getting review bombed for being MIA and no progress in over a year. The patch was promising with a number of new features and maps along side a complete revamp of the Settlement Development Perks - which is exactly the diversity the game needed to introduce some functional diversity in each playthrough. However, the only development perk that was actually available for use was the first level of a settlement when you get 5 burgage plots. This is usually attained in the first couple months of a new settlement, 10-15 minutes into a playthrough. All the other/later features are unavailable and under development.

BUT THEN NOTHING... That hit the Beta branch in Oct 2025. 10 months later and we have not seen 1 single advancement in the development perks. Sure some mechanics systems and features have been reworked slightly since then, bugs have been fixed, etc., but 10 months later and I am unable to go back and play the game without it feeling basically the exact same as my last playthrough 9 months ago. It feels a lot like all those promises from October were just to stop the bleed from the review bombing, but I cannot say they have held up to what they promised the community 10 months ago.

The Pro's:
-The game is beautiful
-The medieval lord experience is immersive
-The game is fairly intuitive and has a very useable UI

The Con's:
-The replayability is horrible. There was actually more diversity and options before they blew up the old development perk system.
-Development speed is atrocious. At this rate this game will still be in early access in 2030
-$40 is way too much for this game in its current state

However the process of starting another village is awful and tedious, and pointlessly slow. Trade between regions that you control has to be equivalent in value, which means you cannot send resources to help your new villages unless you send an equivalent amount of value in goods back -  which is impossible for a new village for several years. You essentially have to restart the game for each region you settle in, with no shortcuts. 

By the time it is possible to set up trades, you could have just generated enough wealth through vegetable farming to buy anything you need from the global trading system, and the whole thing falls apart. Why bother building wide when you can build tall? Just put everything you need in one town. But then why have the regions at all? What is their purpose, apart from as an abstract victory condition. 

There's a lot of potential here but the game really doesn't know what it wants to be doing at the macro scale. I'm sure it can be fixed but I don't really think it's worth playing until some of this stuff gets sorted out.

Manor Lords is a beautiful game with a gorgeous presentation and a detailed simulation.  At its heart, it is a competent city builder with a more historical flair that slides in RTS elements and rewards players for fine tuning an economy and building it up as rapidly as possible.

Unfortunately, the game does not give players the necessary tools to perform the fine tuning without it feeling like a real hassle, and a number of bugs that have persisted since launch have gone unfixed, while new content is being added.  There is no way to lock families from being automatically employed when shifting the work force around, while keeping specific families unemployed is important to managing production chains and construction projects.  Resources are physicalized everywhere in this game except for the last mile between marketplaces and residences, which is very counter-intuitive and results in very confusing and frustrating logistical issues cropping up.  Getting supplies to marketplaces is finicky and inconsistent.  All progression and development relies on logistics that are frustrating to manage without the UI or the tools to do so or figure out what's going wrong.  Your houses will magically lack access to supplies when supplies appear to be available.  Your warehouse and logistical workers will sit around doing nothing.  And you will not know why.

It seems the developer has retreated to an echo chamber Discord to gather all of their feedback on development of the game, a Discord consisting of players with hundreds of hours who have found a variety of creative and inconvenient ways to get around bugs and don't see an issue with the game as it currently stands.  Attempting to give any feedback contrary to this echo chamber results in getting shouted out or ignored.  It seems unlikely the issues with this game's logistical simulation will be addressed any time soon, and it's a real shame, because if logistics in this title were actually manageable I would give it a strong recommendation. 

 So much of the gameplay relies heavily on core mechanics that just do not feel good, and seem to function inconsistently or in highly counter intuitive ways.  This disrupts the flow of the experience and results in frustration.  As it is, purchasing Manor Lords will result in feeling like you just spent 40$ on a broken game, and based on the direction I see development going since I purchased this title, it's not entirely clear if it will be fixed.  Perhaps I will update this review later if logistics issues get resolved, but until then, I will have to give it a thumb down.

I have been playing for 18 hours and currently encounter three issues. I hope developers can pay attention to:
1. The main city is unable to assist in the development of affiliated villages:
I created an affiliated village. Apart from initial supplies, the main town has no other way to "donate" supplies to help it develop rapidly. Resulting in the later stage, although the main town was very prosperous, it could only rely on the slow development of villages in other areas through barter. In the event of natural or man-made disasters, if supplies are urgently needed, we can only act hastily. Players who were about to "enjoy themselves" in the later stages of operation are still feeling frustrated.
2. There is no opportunity for redevelopment after the population returns to zero:
My village is developing slowly. The village was attacked by mountain bandits, and there was no army, or the army did not have time to defend. It was burned down, and supplies were returned to zero. The villagers went hungry and all ran away. Although the damaged house can be repaired, there is a lack of materials, and satisfaction has dropped to 2%. If it's the main town, it may have to be reopened. But I encountered this problem in an affiliated village. At this point, the main town is also unable to "provide relief" to this poor village. Ultimately, it resulted in a population return to zero, while satisfaction remained at 2%, thus failing to attract new villagers. In the end, this becomes a ghost village, and the post game experience is too poor.
3. Traffic jams at trade stations result in money and nowhere to spend:
I have opened many trade routes, and too many merchants' carriages have caused congestion at the trade stations. If an additional trading station is opened, they will only recognize the nearest trading station and cannot do any diversion. Even if the trade strategy chooses "no trade", it cannot prevent enthusiastic merchants from driving empty carriages to stroll. And I can't close the trade route either. In the end, despite the fact that the region was wealthy, the commercial flow deteriorated due to merchants blocking the trading stations.

To solve the above three problems, I provide some suggestions for developers to refer to:
1. Can a material resolution be added to facilitate the lord to spend his own money on delivering a portion of the resources from a certain town to other villages, thereby promoting rapid development in the surrounding area, or funding the reconstruction of the disaster stricken areas in the surrounding area?
After all, it can be understood that regional wealth is not circulating, and the lord's money cannot still circulate throughout the entire map?
2. Can we consider a default satisfaction rate of 50% for a population of 0? In this way, even with zero population, there is still an opportunity to attract new villagers to settle in, gradually revitalizing the village.
Or, in the case of zero population, can it be allowed to redeploy worker camps in the area to supplement the population and supplies?
3. Can the setting of trade routes be refined, allowing players to close or make other adjustments to reduce the number of merchants?
Or, could it be to change the rules of the trading station to allow a specific type of item to be exclusively traded at a trading station, in order to facilitate the diversion of different merchants for players?

I really want to love this game, and I think there is a strong core / framework / foundation for the city-building, but unfortunately everything outside of that feels woefully shallow and/or unfinished. That's understandable in an EA title, but even in the newest beta update (which I understand is mostly refactoring/reorganizing) these kinds of core issues aren't addressed to any degree. 

In short, the good/great:

- Great city-building mechanics
- Interesting resource allocation, management and progression
- Very cool building tile system and specifically the use of core burghs/houses which can upgrade several levels or be specialized
- Interesting new perk and environment system which looks promising, but only available through a single perk (for now)
- The scale and building animations are great

The bad:

- Diplomacy is non-existent and shouldn't even be in the game in it's current state
- The UI is clunky at best. It desperately needs an update for things like the Help pages, where tabbed content doesn't have any kind of logical organization and you can't search, only to find in many cases extremely vague and curt descriptions some of which end with where this resource comes from but don't bother stating what it's used for and what you do with it (like Wax).
- Population management becomes a chore and there's no menu that lists out all the families in a town and lets you unassign at will, instead forcing you to meticulously point-and-click search through buildings to see where spare families might be. This becomes very unwieldy once you reach 40+ families.
- Family assignment to buildings is too simplistic, and inevitably causes you to babysit buildings like farmhouses where workers are only relevant for 6/12 months of the year. Since you can't assign a family to multiple roles with any kind of priority/seasonal system (farm until harvest, plow/sow, then go chop wood during winter instead of sitting around doing nothing for the next 9 months) you have to heavily micro-manage.
- Resource nodes are too scattershot and random in the region-system of the game. As of the beta you're guaranteed to at least get stone and food, but if you don't have rich iron, clay, or etc, you have no way to gain these except trading, where fees are exorbitant and trickle even with 4 traders on horses is very slow.

Unfortunately I could go on and on with more and more nitpicks, and it feels like this is yet another case of an indie game with fantastic potential that is simply trying to cram too many mechanics into itself instead of having a more concentrated and focused core gameplay loop. Maybe this will change in the future with the newer team and all this refactoring and promise of smaller more consistent updates, but as of now, it struggles under the weight of it's own ambition.

I'm giving it a Recommended, but a very tentative one. There's a lot of potential here from someone clearly very talented, and it's a smart idea to get a team together, but the game desperately needs entire sections of itself (almost every aspect of the in-game UI, diplomacy, etc) overhauled or replaced because it feels and very obviously is placeholder content.

Fundamentally this is a really relaxing city builder, with some solid underlying ideas of being able to follow your citizens around while they do their tasks. Tasks generally do not get completed unless someone is actually working on them, so switching takes time if someone is far away from their new workplace etc. Or if they're busy with their fields at home they perform less in the workplace. There are a lot of aspects of these mechanics that are enjoyable and relaxing.
But it also has a lot of issues. 
1) Combat is often decided by bugs and fundamental issues. Battles are suddenly won without doing anything, or by just defeating one of multiple groups of enemies and then the game thinks they are all defeated. AI often seems to have unlimited funds and prepping for combat is as easy as just buying all the mercs so the AI doesn't get to buy all the mercs.
2) Physical distance and time correlate very badly, a merchant walking from place to place may take months to bring over a couple of weeks worth of produce, people may take days to walk to their workplace. For example when the farm starts going into harvesting season people might arrive 5 or 6 days later.
It's still impossible to just send stuff over from one village to another. It needs to be done by bartering or trade. This is a choice I guess, but bartering prices and quantities can't be set making it very impractical.
3) Lots of tiny bugs: Oxen get stuck, burgage plots suddenly don't snap to roads or other plots in a certain territory, people do nothing without identifyable causes.
4) economic techtrees are unfinished and do not lead to variation in gameplay so the basic mechanism is just to check what unlimited resource you have and start mining and selling that as early as possible; wait ; win.

So I was disappointed to find multiple types of meat and fruit and produce now and still lots of issues in the fundamental mechanics. I do not need more stuff, I need the stuff that's there to work better and then build more interesting stuff on top of a solid base.

The story being sold is better than the game being shipped...

Manor Lords is one of the most effective marketing campaigns in recent gaming memory. Over 3 million wishlists before launch. A "solo developer, 7 years, one man's dream" narrative that every outlet happily repeated. Trailers and gameplay videos showing a deep, living medieval world.

Then you actually play it.

What you get is a shallow, repetitive city-builder with a handful of systems stretched thin across hours of nothing happening. The depth the trailers promised isn't hiding somewhere you haven't unlocked yet. It simply isn't in the game. You hit the ceiling fast, and once you're there, there's no reason to keep playing.

Here's the part that bothers me. The "solo dev" framing this game rode to 3 million copies sold isn't quite what it looks like. The credits list contractors for art, animation, extra programming, motion capture, and more. Even the developer has said the criticism of the solo label is fair. So strip away the underdog story, and what you're left with is a game that had years of development, outside help, an Epic MegaGrant, Patreon funding, and tens of millions in revenue, and it still feels this empty.

I don't know what to call that. I know what it doesn't feel like, which is a team pouring everything they have into delivering on what they sold you.

If you're considering buying it, do two things first. Ignore the trailers, because they're a promise the game doesn't keep. And look at when the last real content update landed, not patches, actual content. Then ask yourself if that pace matches a game that's sold over 3 million copies.

For me, the answer was a hard NO. There are better city-builders at lower prices made by teams being honest about who they are. Spend your money there.

I genuinely struggle to find the words to describe the joy this game brings me.
Maybe it's because I'm a nerd who loves anything with a medieval setting
Maybe it's because I've always loved town/city builders and battle strategy games
Maybe it's because I got invested early, taking part in the open beta, patreon, discord, and twitter conversations with Greg, just for the chance to leave a mark on a game that got me more excited than any other game ever has.

But all that aside, this game makes me [i] feel [/i] how immersive RPGs make me feel. It makes me care about the world and makes me feel like I'm making a difference, and it makes me mourn when my lumberjack from the very first settlers camp dies in defence of his home, or worse, guilt when he falls on campaign to win some land off another noble.
Watching your village burn in any other similar game is annoying. Watching your village burn in Manor Lords is harrowing and tragic.

This game is beautiful.
You probably don't need me telling you that.. But the attention to detail and historical grounding goes a long way for people like me. Together with the gorgeously unique seasons and the wonder of Unreal, very few games (if any) surpass Manor Lords in its ability to make me stop, (Ctrl + C,) and appreciate the scene for a moment.

Gameplay-wise, the number of resources and complexity of resource management is just right for me. No Anno resource chains and trade routes that take a chartered accountant to keep track of, no glaring gameplay gaps where the illusion breaks nor incentive to mindlessly scale in and endless, stressful loop. Managing my village just seems to make sense, where if something goes wrong, it's almost always because of something that [i] could [/i] and [i] should [/i] go wrong because of my mistakes, or chance. And when something goes right, it's incredibly rewarding.

The Music is fantastic
The battles are shockingly impressive considering they're somewhat of an afterthought in a game that's not even trying to be a 'Total War Killer'

Whatever Greg has in mind for the finished product, if the game so far is anything to go off of, I trust it'll continue to provide me many [b] many [/b] more hours of enjoyment.

Thanks Greg, and everyone who helped bring this project to life
You have every reason to be proud of what you've made.

I really wanted to recommend Manor Lords. After 318 hours, I can't.

Manor Lords is one of the most beautiful and compelling medieval city builders I've played. The organic roads, burgage plots, seasons, farming, livestock, production and ability to equip an army from your own economy create an incredible medieval settlement. The idea of this game is fantastic.
Unfortunately, the further you progress, the more obvious it becomes that the underlying economic simulation simply does not work well enough to support the game built around it.

My latest settlement has roughly 700 people, over 100 sheep, huge apple orchards, multiple tailors, extensive industry, and three fully staffed trading posts with four horses each. I'm producing enormous surpluses of spears, shields, chainmail, helmets, tools, coal and other manufactured goods and exporting everything I reasonably can.

Yet somehow this enormous settlement cannot reliably provide basic clothing and beverages.
Imports of things like oats and salt consume virtually all of the revenue generated by exporting manufactured goods. I can't afford to import enough fruit, vegetables or livestock to supplement local production. Royal Tax has pushed my treasury roughly 10,000 into debt despite eventually taxing my population at an absurd 40%, which means I can't afford to settle another region to produce the flax, grain and oats that would reduce my dependence on imports.

This creates a ridiculous circular problem:
Need basic goods → need imports → imports consume treasury → can't establish another region → can't produce missing resources → must continue importing → debt gets worse.
Building more infrastructure doesn't necessarily solve it. More tailors don't magically fix clothing. More beverage production doesn't fix beverage supply despite huge raw-material stocks. I built THREE fully staffed trading posts with TWELVE horses between them and saw little meaningful improvement in trade throughput.

That's the fundamental problem with Manor Lords right now. When I encounter a shortage, I want to identify the bottleneck, invest in solving it, and see my economy respond. Too often the game simply doesn't.

I returned because of the latest major update hoping the economy had matured. Instead, my late-game experience feels more broken than before. New resources, livestock requirements and production chains have been added while the underlying trade and economic systems still struggle to support large settlements.

And that's incredibly frustrating because I love what Manor Lords is trying to be. There is nothing else quite like watching a tiny medieval village organically develop into a large town, supplying its industries and raising armies from its own population.

But after 318 hours, I've reached the point where I just want to finish a campaign and earn the Large City victory. Instead of being challenged by interesting strategic decisions, I'm fighting systems that increasingly feel unfinished or poorly balanced.

Manor Lords began development years ago and has tremendous potential, but potential eventually has to become a functioning game. Adding more systems doesn't help if the existing ones don't work together at scale.

I love the latest patches adding Fishing ponds the UE-5 update and clear communication as well as a very helpful friendly community.

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]
Overall, Manor Lords is a standout title that successfully combines strategic depth with immersive medieval simulation. It’s a game that rewards patience and strategic thinking, and it’s clear that a lot of passion and skill went into its creation. I debated on buying this game for a while. And even though this review is a yes to buy it, I have a few things I want to mention.

First, the developer has created a game that is extremely accurate to the historical medieval period. This doesn't lend well to the modern gaming mindset. This game is something only a history nerd like myself can get into, I feel like your average gamer is going to get a taste of it and move on.

Second, the developer has spent a lot of time making this game beautiful! You can zoom in on anything and the detail is just amazing! But I feel like because of this, things like tutorials have taken a back seat. I had to restart the game no less than six times to begin to understand some of the mechanics going on here. And I'm not going to get into the insanity that is what happens if you don't upgrade your homes!

Third is the frustrating parts like, I had to figure out that "Emmer" means "Wheat". Why are there two different names for it? I had to give up on any kind of trade because it's not financially viable when you have to pay to open up a trade route for every single commodity. Got a bumper crop of wheat, I mean Emmer? Well, you can't sell it until you grease the merchant's palms apparently. Finally got the supply chain for Linen up and running? Too bad, pay the merchant before you can sell it outside of your lands.

And I guess you could say that this is what I came here to say. This game is frustrating in that you have so many different hurdles to jump just to be able to get a functioning economy and to be able to field a passable militia that it's kind of ridiculous. Almost every territory is lacking in ore to the point of being laughable. My best run on this game had me using 116 ore to try and defend the village while also supplying tools just to keep the economy going. I did well enough against the random bandits, but taking another territory? Impossible. I had 3 units at half strength or less when the iron ran out and the enemy was fielding 7 units at full strength, that is until his 3 mercenary units arrived!

What about economic victory? LOL, what? Even when I had the salt mine I couldn't get any economic traction because I'm paying for the trade route and then paying an extra 10 to buy anything, plus the building, plus the animals, plus the people. And for some reason salt isn't very high value? I'm a NERD, I know the meaning of the phrase "below the salt".  I'm also a gardener and the thought of PAYING for seeds in an agrarian society? I still have favorite seeds from tomatoes that I planted more than ten years ago. They're still viable! Jeez, they pulled seeds out of ancient tombs and got them to germinate! I'm suppose to pay 38 for carrot seeds? Come on, get real.

All of this is to say that this game is very enjoyable if you don't want to do anything with your village past getting it to be functional. Any attempt to go beyond your own borders is going to leave your troops dead on the field. And you will feel every death in the loss of productivity. If you're lucky enough to get a territory with an unlimited supply of iron from the beginning then you may have a chance. But I don't think this is what the developer had planned because I never had that happen. I think you're supposed to build up and then take a territory with unlimited iron deposits. And that would be fine if I wasn't also trying to keep the economy running by providing tools for everyone.

Also, what is it with the lack of births? Why am I waiting for new families to settle all of the time? Can we have some weddings and start with the procreation? And that brings me to the timeline for things. People can build things fast and get a lot done in a short amount of time but dealing with taking territory or fighting battles in less than the first year? "Hey Bob, I see you finally got your house built now grab your spear and shield we're off to war!" Are the bandits inside the village or is it their relatives? Who is helping them steal and get away with it? We've got 7 families and everyone should know everyone else but somehow those rabbits we shot yesterday disappeared? Shouldn't a dog have barked at least? Can we not use the militia for a night watch or something? It's not like they're attacking en masse, grab the thief and cut off a finger!  No, you have to spend days traveling and not working to destroy the bandit camp and possibly die.

I will keep playing this game because I'm intrigued. As a medieval history nerd, this game is the closest thing to replicating actual medieval life in a game and I find that fascinating. I only hope that the developer will continue to tweak, start putting in more than one sentence explanations for things, and maybe explain things better in the tutorials. I think the bones of a truly awesome game are here, but there is still a lot of work to be done.

[b]The not as good - [/b] It's not finished yet, some of the upcoming mechanics are hinted at ( experience for individual retinue soldier, increased policies etc... ), trade ( as you might expect at the start of EA ) is a little imbalanced, and you hit the tipping point ( players of Total War games will know what I mean ) fairly quickly in terms of military power leaving you with the expansion of your village/towns as the end goal.

[b]Buy it or not ?[/b] I was one of the bazillion people who wishlisted this. I also have xbox game pass so could  have got it for free, but I still bought it in the hope that the Dev would get enough cash in to continue delivering his vision. I love where this game looks to be going. It is in a very good state for an early access title, but it is lacking some longevity at the moment so I will likely only check back in to play after major updates. I am super excited for the end product. So I would say if you want to support the Dev to continue delivering his vision, buy it with your eyes open and help support it on the understanding it's not finished but still very playable. If you're more risk averse, wait till launch when hopefully we'll all be blown away by what is delivered :)

[h3]Detailed observations[/h3]

[b]Things I love[/b]
*This game is beautiful... Playing it on 4070 with everything maxed out, the level of detail is incredible. The lighting, the way the terrain reacts to the weather ( rain, snow, wind ), little details like creatures running and flying in the countryside. If you were playing on a VR headset and stuck a cow pat on your desk for the authentic aroma you might believe you were out in the countryside ! :)
*Things like your villagers running away screaming when brigands get close add immersion
*Building system is brilliant. Seriously I love the way placing housing works.
*Being able to zoom in to the level of seeing individuals and the work they're doing, even your oxen !
*The agriculture model is very nice... Effectively models fertility and crop rotation ( even if it is a little confusion at first)
*The third person spectate function is a wonderful touch and gives you a great way to explore your village
*Sounds and audio are fantastic

[b]Things which need finishing or improving[/b] ( all of these I would deem to be usual sort of issues when a game is released to EA. The whole point of EA is to get more eyes playing the game to spot stuff )
*Balance
- Baron takes territory too readily
- Trade is imbalanced making it too easy to get money, but without the money it's hard to defeat the baron so overall balance is in need of tuning
- Unit balance needs finalising... Archers seem underwhelming at the moment
*Pathing - Your units sometimes take some whacky routes and don't follow the easiest roads which can be a problem when your village is attacked by brigands
*Collision detection - units can walk through your castle wall but not the gate 
*QoL improvements - Being able to get more detail on what the order of the building queue is and where bottlenecks are in production more easily are good examples... 
*Policies need to be fleshed out more. There are currently only a few switched on
*Development points tree needs tuning and balancing
*Manor building needs work and fixing ( see aforementioned pathing comment. There's no point in the walls other than for the looks at the moment. 

Overall I'm really happy with the state of the game given it's EA status. There's clearly a lot of stuff to be completed / new stuff to be added so I hope that Greg will be posting some plans for future updates and functionality in the near future so we can all see where he is going with this. I'm sure that after all the hype of the launch, it's going to take some time to process the flood of feedback but from what I've seen so far the engagement model is fantastic so I'm really hopeful that this will become a fully fleshed out and fantastic title at launch. 

Thanks for reading if you made it this far !

as a PURE feudal city builder sim I think Manor Lords is actually amazing.  The presentation is great, love the music (that one dude just going nuts on the flute always makes me giggle), the zoning system is cool and there's a great diversity of building types that sort of randomizes their appearance so you don't wind up with row after row of identical-looking burgage plots.

The most recent update did away with the awful perk system that locked away building types and really shackled the player's ability to experiment, and the new system is a much more organic, iterative sort of affinity system which I think is a massive improvement.  I'm still on the fence about whether I like the region system as well...I like that the resources are dispersed across the map, but sometimes you get spawns that just make you want to cry...why does it always have to be rich clay 😭....I know it's random but if just FEELS like I never get a good one.

I don't believe the intent of this game is to allow the player to build massive metropolises and gigantic citadels, but I worry that if that sort of thing becomes possible as a late-game goal, the economy would be so byzantine it would be tedious and confusing to most players, very much at risk of becoming a spreadsheet sort of game rather than a chill city builder.  If the scope can stay tight and focused I think it could wind up being one of the better examples of this genre.  And based on how the early access started and where it is now, I really like the direction this game is going in.

Manor Lords is one of those gems that is still being polished to be the brightest of all the city builders out there. It's one of the best in the market already, however, this doesn't mean that everything is going perfectly.

It's a really intuitive game and easy to get going with. You build and grow your settlement according to your needs. In the early stage, you gather resources, later you produce or buy the resources. Want more population? Build houses. It's a city-builder that follows the rules book.

It presents various scenarios, one most focused on the city-building aspect of the game, the other on the military, and finally, another that is a mix of the two. Every single one of them has great aspects and lets the player deal with everything that the game has to offer. However, that brings up a real problem that I have with Manor Lords. It feels slow and repetitive... I found myself without the patience to finish a scenario just because when you reach some stability you're just doing the same thing over and over.

Military-wise, once again, it's simple. You don't really have to think much about strategy itself. If you have a bigger army and well-equipped troops you're gonna win. Otherwise, you're probably gonna lose.

It is one of the most beautiful games that I had the opportunity to play this year. It creates a great environment! Just watch the images that the developer shows on the Steam page, the seasons passing and the population working. It is a really good.

Still has a long way to go before becoming the best out there. I decided to don't go deep into bugs since we are talking about early access. Bugs are expected and you shall just report them and hope they get patched the soon as possible. Never had anything game breaking in my expirience.

Do I believe that it's worth spending €39.99 on Manor Lords? NO. At least not right now, however, if you find a good promotion give it a try.

[h1] The game is still in an early alpha stage. [/h1]
Yet you have to pay 40 bucks. It severely lacks in features and polish. I enjoyed it thoroughly for a while but when you've dug deep enough everything cracks at the seam. You realize what you thought was a deep well of fun was a shallow puddle with a label slapped on top promising it will be a vast lake eventually. There's simply not enough depth. To explain everything would take too long so here's the short of it. 

Your aim is to build a large self-sustaining town. To get there you need food, fuel and regional wealth. To get all of that you take resources from the region you're in to either feed and fuel your town or to sell in a trading post to mass regional wealth. Food and fuel is needed to keep your population alive. Regional wealth is required to upgrade your buildings, earn tax revenue and import goods that your population needs. During this process bandits and an opposing baron's soldiers will randomly spawn somewhere on the edge of the map to mess up your stuff. You stop them by having weapons and armor crafted and equipped by your villagers, making them a militia. You also buy retainers and mercenaries with tax money. You use said armies to defend your stuff. But you can also use your army to expand into different regions. Making a claim on a region requires influence, which you can get with a tithe, essentially a tax on your surplus of food.  Making a claim will spawn an army of the opposing baron that you have to beat and badabing that region is yours. That's more or less the gist of it. 

There's no diplomacy, but devs said there will be in the future. A tech tree with as of now very few options and no real end game. There's almost no variation when it comes to military, and no defense buildings like city walls, moats or castles.. No NPC cities to conquer or trade with. The whole map is more or less void of any activity except a few bandit camps that don't do much of anything except steal your stuff sometimes. The game is also riddled with bugs and crashes. If you don't save often you lose a lot of progress.

The game has a strong foundation. The way your villagers work and move throughout the town you've built is a technological marvel. Building your city is seamless, efficient and easy. It's very satisfying to see every individual NPC go about their days. The game just needs more than a foundation, it needs a whole building. After that you can slap a 40 dollar price tag on it. Until then, I wouldn't buy it.

I played the game when it came out and decided to give it another go once it'd gained more subtance. Alas, a year later, that extra substance isn't quite there yet. 
There are many many things this game does well, from the graphics to the gridless urbanism, but at this stage, it still mostly feels like a demo, with too many things alluded to but still not there... Judging by the progress over the first year, it might take a while to get the kind of city described in the main illustration.
Gameplay-wise, It also takes forever to get anything done, so a lot of your time will be spent looking at your lone cow dragging a single log at a time out of the 8 needed from one side of the map to the other. Time acceleration ought to alleviate this but alas, doing so might get in the way of the mandatory micromanagement of every single of your individual working villagers. Get distracted and miss the critical window for harvest and sowing, and your settlement will be toast. I'm yet to find any trace of the "complex economic and social simulations" referred to in the synopsis, but I can still roleplay hide & seek with my villagers to find out where they are vs. where they ought to be.
Some current game decisions also seem odd, like farming in a medieval society being apparently a 3 months a year job for a minority of the population, with hunting-gathering almost more efficient, or churches devoid of any clergy...
Still, that game deserves to succeed, and I'll probably check it again in a year. In the meantime, if you're on the fence, there might be games more deserving of your time and money, like the excellent Urbek.

MANOR LORDS IS DEAD
I see a clear pattern here that tells me Manor Lords is now dead: an enthusiast and his team are working on it, led by a perfectionist who both gets lost in the details and reaches for the stars. Manor Lords launched in Early Access, and instead of focusing on finishing the game, they had to upgrade to UE5 first – the best games aren’t beautiful, they work!

The game was a huge financial success, but development has barely moved forward. The last update was a hotfix in January 2025 – six months ago. Since then, all we've seen are discounts. No matter how much money gets poured into the game now, the bulk of the revenue has already been made. The developers know this too.

And so, just like with KSP2, the game will slowly be put to sleep – and we’re right in the middle of it. Everywhere in the game, you can see glimpses of ambitious ideas, the broad scope it once promised. That was surely part of the Early Access strategy: to boost sales.

But when I look at what’s happened over more than a year, it feels like the game might be finished by 2038. And before they waste that much money, they’d rather pull the plug and leave it as-is – just like they did with KSP2.

I’m sad and disappointed, because as always, it’s money that ruined it.

I want to support Greg and Slavic Magic with this review. Even though over the last year I haven't played the game as much, I enjoyed ML when it came out. For me, personally, it was money well spent for the play time I got out of it. 

Yes, there is not enough variability (yet) to lose yourself in this game for hundreds of hours as is the case with some city builders out there (actually, I saw some people clocking hundreds of hours in ML too). Anyway, I don't think there should be a comparison made with other builders, because this game strikes a nice balance between realism and game play mechanics, without adding cards, perks, made up stats, loot chests and other random mechanics to boost up its game play artificially. Part of the reason why people love ML is how REAL, historically immersive its setting is. And I think in this regard, in this respect to its medieval setting, the game outshines many, if not most, others.

But I also want to address one thing that I appreciate wholly and that is often used as a critical point: "No updates".
Really? Slavic Magic has been nothing but transparent about the upcoming updates and changes to their team. The game is NOT abandoned in any way. There were updates.

And more than enough given the circumstances. 

Now I'm not part of their team, so what comes next is mostly my speculation from my personal experience in corporate, IT, gamedev, and whatnot.

I assume it's a very stressful and tough transition from being a solo developer to running and leading a team of other people. It's not a magical "more people = faster development, better product" formula. If that was the case, AAA companies, with hundreds of people on payroll, would not release lackluster products year after year. Coming from a corporate background, I know it, and most of us do. More people = chaos. There is a reason why so many solo and small indie teams are taking over Steam charts. Because it's easier to release a coherent, lovable product when your vision is not muddled by corporate shenanigans.. 

And because small devs LOVE what they do.

I think Slavic Magic is an example of a person who built a product and loved it in every way. 

But he was one man with a singular vision. Now, transferring this vision to a newly-formed team of professional strangers is a @$%#ing tough challenge.

Managing people is HARD. Ensuring the quality of output of multiple people is on par with the vision of a solo game developer who spent years pouring love into his creation is HARD.

From the updates I learned they are revamping existing systems. They make a robust foundation for future updates. I think this is a very solid strategy. If they, instead, would opt to making smaller, piling up incremental updates to please the masses, sooner or later they would've drowned in tech debt, and ran themselves into a corner. To keep this game a masterpiece, grow it, and preserve everything we loved about it during the release is to EXPAND its setting, to grow its scale, and for that you need a good, robust code and systems foundation. We can't possibly expect a solo dev, on their first title, would not cut corners on such a massive product, to even release it is an undertaking most of people never approach. 

Now this version of a product needs to be expanded, and what should he/they do? Add a bunch of low-hanging, incoherent, all over-the-place mechanics and features, to please an odd person here and there? Some people want more walls and towers, some people want to paint shields, some want wolves in the forest and, I don't know, drunkards around the tavern? Who knows what. OK. These features sound good and immersive, but they won't add hours to your game play. Neither they will make this game fundamentally better. Because it's already fundamentally good.

But scaled updates, like combat AI, settlements AI, system overhauls, navigation, maps, and who knows how many other things they are working hard to improve and extend under the hood right, now THAT will allow to grow this game, possibly into something even better.


And here comes THE hammer. 

Greg doesn't owe me "better". Greg owes me nothing. I paid for the medieval city-builder, and I got it. I played and enjoyed it for 50 hours. He could take my money and ran into the sunset for all I care. I didn't buy it because there was some roadmap that promised me something cool in X years. (looking at you, Valheim, and f.. you again, lol)

But with ML, now I'm told there's more in the works. Could be more. In a year this could, or could not, become a game that is so much more, and yet so much like the game I enjoyed. And I already bought it! 

Slavic Magic is still here and wants to give ME more for my money.

And you want me to leave a negative review for that?

I went into this game having already played the demo when that was a thing.
I learned important lessons about food and fuel during that, and thought I was ready for this...

I was wrong.

Things went smoothly for my first 10 or so winters, biding my time and slowly building up.
I managed to keep the supply chain going, having no issues with food, fuel, or other goods needed for upgrades and further expansion.
My subjects were a happy bunch, who worked hard and partied harder.
The forests were well kempt, the fields were flourishing, and people had the extras a plenty.

The one thing I failed to account for was the brigands, who decided I was a juicy target.
Their first band was beaten by the Baron's army before they even got to my territory, a great success for my unprepared militia.
A couple of springs later, they returned in force. My militia was even less prepared for this attack, and ended up being nuked by the bastards. They proceeded to destroy nearly the entire village, and stole most of my food-stores.

I worked diligently to rebuild the lost homes, workplaces, markets, and church.
The loss of all that food resulted in the village starving from October onwards, and it didn't get any better after that following fall's harvest.
My people spent yet another winter starving, but steadfast and faithful that the situation would improve.
Boy were they wrong.

Following that winter's starvation, the brigands came once more during the summer.
New crops were well on their way, and things had the potential to look bright.
The people's (and mine as a result) hopes and dreams were crushed in yet another devastating battle for my reformed militia and tiny retinue.

It was a massacre. The blood of poor farmers, cobblers, hunters, brewers, loggers, and many more was spilled across the houses and fields. The young were annihilated in the second sacking of the church. The manor's walls were swiftly torn down. The burgages, farmhouses, and markets were burned to a fine crisp. The pandemonium was palpaple as I hopelessly watched all I built be torn to the ground.

To round of the brigand's attack, that bastard Baron decided now was the time to claim my land. He swiftly moved in and finished of the remaining brigands, and destroyed what little the brigands had yet to destroy of my now defenceless village.
I could only watch in 12x speed horror, as his army celebrated on what once was a bustling, up-and-coming, town.

The pain in my heart is untenable, my sorrow unquechable, my desire for revenge impossible to ignore.
I will avenge this loss in my next attempt at besting that Robber-Baron, I swear on my un-born children's soul that it will be done.

Game is well worth its current price. 10/10, would die to brigands and starvation again.

It is a very interesting game, but it does have several game breaking bugs. Now, I did play the Beta version, and that may have been the contributing factor. 
I like the RTS/Citybuilder combo, and the city builder part works fine, but the RTS doesn't work very well.

Here are the following issues I have encountered that might break the game:

1: Retinue can't get out of manor house, because a bunch of people are just standing in the doorway forever, which lets bandit camps pillage your stuff and when you are attacked by raiders, well, you are fudged.

2: building a wall around your city blocks off building anything, yup, you can't build inside the city walls.

3: units get fatigued very quickly from running, as in, you run for 2-3 days and you loose 30% of your fatigue, but it then takes them several weeks if not more than a month to recover.

4: Units appear like they can wear armour, but even though I have the armour and helmets, they only put on the helmets.

On the Citybuilder/management side there are a few things that are equally game breaking:

1: I have 180 charcoal/firewood in my storage, but it never gets distributed.

2: food is too scarce for larger settlements on some maps, I played high peaks, and I was lucky enough to start with mushrooms and animals for hunting, but there is only poor farmland and no fish, so once I got above 18 households or families, they started to starve, didn't have enough people to farm, and even if I did, it would just have required even more food than they would make due to the poor farmland.

As soon as all those things are improved/fixed, the game will be playable.

The most recent update fixed all of the performance related issues I was having and I am back to enjoying the game the way I used to. I am VERY HAPPY with the updates to the engine and core systems. I know that you are receiving many negative reviews from people who are complaining about slow release of game features but please know that experienced gamers like myself are impressed that you have put fundamentals first and are choosing to optimize first before just rolling out new content that isn't scaleable.

The improvements to the resource systems have made developing towns more intuitive. You now need to engage with all of the core mechanics in order to succeed broadly, and those systems are no longer frustrating to engage with. The updates to customizing production limits and brackets for trade and industry and specialists has put an end to the pausing and unpausing of extensions. All very good.

Suggestions:

Automatic crop rotation is still not quite ideal as it does not allow you to pre-plow fallow fields earlier in the season prior to harvest and planting. With such limited time to harvest and plant it is important to be able to plow fallow fields in spring without having to disable the crop rotation automation. Setting worker areas for farms should work like drawing a boundary, not like a circle that gets bigger or smaller. I still feel like I spend an inordinate amount of time microing farmhouse allocations and field designations.

Castle planner is still clunky and because it is high-stakes resource wise, it can be extremely frustrating when something goes wonky. 

BIGGEST SUGGESTION:

Let people customize resource starts during game creation. I know you want people to adapt to whatever they're given, but I don't always want to play the hand I'm dealt for hours upon hours. Sometimes I just really want a region with fertile fields and a quarry so I can build pretty castles and farms. I shouldn't have to restart and regenerate maps over and over to play the kind of game I want. Let people curate the kind of experience they want to have.

Keep up the great work. Awesome game.
